items.title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
items.desc: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous open problem for 167 years, with a proof formalized in Lean that spans over 250,000 pages. Just hours later, Stanford researchers published an independent, entirely human competing proof, and mathematicians are now checking whether either one holds up. The article Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem. Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement . According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well. Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line. To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line. Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says. Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo. "It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said. Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away. About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote. Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. items.title: OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
items.desc: OpenAI has significantly strengthened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In adaptive red-teaming tests, the success rate for extracting protected reasoning fell from 54 percent to 0.2 percent. The company is also suspending thousands to tens of thousands of accounts each week over coordinated distillation campaigns. The article OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says . The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too. The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems combine targeted training, input and output filters for messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly. Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red teaming against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower is better. Ad Anthropic is fighting systematic distillation attacks as well , also banning tens of thousands of accounts to curb the theft of internal reasoning, reportedly succeeding in 90 to 99 percent of cases. items.title: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats
items.desc: Signal is blocking screenshots to stop AI agents like Apple's Siri AI, Google's Gemini Intelligence, and Meta's Muse from reading private chats. The app calls it an "existential threat" to privacy, but admits its protections remain incomplete, including on macOS. Apple, Google, and Microsoft should follow suit. The article Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat" to privacy. OS-level AI like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture screen content to complete user tasks. That undermines end-to-end encryption by letting agents pull decrypted messages straight from the display and process them externally. Meta's AI agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions, including accessibility tools and screenshots on macOS. Meta says this happened only with explicit user permission. Ad Signal already blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but calls its defenses incomplete: macOS screenshots can't be reliably blocked, and AI access to file systems and notifications remains a risk. Signal says Apple, Google, and Microsoft should make it easy to block AI agents from apps entirely. Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.desc: From July through September 2026, the WordPress Community organized 39 events with the financial support of the project’s five Global Partners: Jetpack, WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Bluehost, and Hostinger. items.full: From July through September 2026, the WordPress Community organized 39 events with the financial support of the project’s five Global Partners : Jetpack, WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Bluehost, and Hostinger. From a small gathering of 56 in Mannheim to a Contributor Day in the Philippines that drew 322 people, and the first-ever WordCamp in Eket, Nigeria, these events brought newcomers, contributors, and builders together around the world. The 39 events were too many to cover in one post, so this recap highlights a few of the moments that stood out. The quarter opened in July with WordCamp Mannheim , a small event with real range. The 56 attendees covered topics from AI and WordPress block development to current security know-how, along with presentations on values, training, and the open web. In August, the momentum moved to Nigeria, where Eket held its inaugural WordCamp on August 15 under the theme “From Idea to Income: Building Opportunities with WordPress.” Engr. Aniebiet Udoh took the stage for the keynote, challenging attendees to embrace the global reach of the web: “The internet has no small towns.” He urged creators to follow a five-step path: Later in August, WordCamp Philippines drew approximately 434 attendees, contributors and first-time attendees, to Iloilo City on August 28-29. One of the highlights of Contributor Day was the Open Source Library, an activity inspired by the Human Library concept. Instead of borrowing a book, participants could “borrow” a person and spend time having a meaningful conversation about their experiences, careers, communities, and journeys in open source. WordPress.com ran both a booth and a dedicated Community + Education table. The education table alone generated connections with 14 schools and universities, sparked three new meetup applications, and produced a new Campus Connect application from Colegio San Agustin in Bacolod. In Uganda, WordPress is reaching people who have never worked with it before. The third edition of WordCamp Masaka welcomed students and first-timers to participate in a hands-on WordPress Practical session. Led by community members, Stephen Dumba and Cinderella Mbabazi, Florence Namyalo , the Founder and CEO of RAPCIO, and the IT team of Equator University of Science and Technology, the group installed WordPress, explored the dashboard, and began building websites. In September, nearly half of this year’s participants at WordCamp Jinja were students. One of them, fascinated by the WordPress ecosystem and its spirit of generosity and inclusivity, drew all the sponsor logos by hand so he could remember them after the event. In September, WordCamp Costa Rica brought together 327 people. A noteworthy highlight was the pre-event WordPress Studio workshop, where 25 participants each built and launched a live site on WordPress.com in a single morning. The event also demonstrated the growing pipeline from education to community. At least 100 attendees came to WordCamp Costa Rica after first experiencing WordPress through WordPress Campus Connect events at Beenova and UCR Esparza earlier in the year. items.title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
items.desc: Nvidia researchers argue that language models often don't need their full context windows—which are slow, expensive, and prone to errors—and propose an alternative. In tests, periodic summaries and targeted keyword search usually matched full-context results at a fraction of the cost. The team even proposes a new class of models that works with short notes instead of long context. The article Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well. A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. Today, GPT 5.6 Sol handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace." Already a subscriber? items.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
items.desc: The Lean and Mathlib community has officially confirmed Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis as correct. Dozens of independent verifiers checked the 17 million lines of computer code. The solution arrived years earlier than expected: Terence Tao had predicted it wouldn't happen until around 2050 and didn't expect AI to solve it alone. The article Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community said in a statement . Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean , a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website . The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper. Ad The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes , forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so." Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in
